title: Genesis 26:1–16
context: A second famine sends Isaac to Gerar, where the Lord appears, forbids Egypt, and reiterates Abraham’s oath of presence, land, and worldwide blessing. Isaac settles, repeats the “sister” lie over Rebekah, is exposed and protected by Abimelech, then prospers a hundredfold until Philistine envy sends him away.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Arminian and Reformed writers of the past on famine, the oath to Isaac, and the sister-ruse at Gerar, in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Sojourn in this land—There was a famine in Jacob's days, and God bid him go down into Egypt, Gen 46:3,4, a famine in Isaac's days, and God bid him not go down: a famine in Abraham's days, and God left him to his liberty, directing him neither way, which (considering that Egypt was always a place of trial to God's people) some ground upon the different characters of these three patriarchs. Abraham was a man of very intimate communion with God, and to him all places and conditions were alike;
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 26:2)

reformed.quote: I do not doubt but a reason is here given why Isaac rather went to the country of Gerar than to Egypt, which perhaps would have been more convenient for him; but Moses teaches that he was withheld by a heavenly oracle, so that a free choice was not left him. It may here be asked, why does the Lord prohibit Isaac from going to Egypt, whither he had suffered his father to go?

verses.text: There was a famine in the land, in addition to the first famine that was in the days of Abraham. Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines, to Gerar.
verses.arminianNotes:
A second famine, after Abraham’s, presses Isaac toward Gerar and Abimelech’s court. Hunger locates a choice of where to sojourn.

Arminians hear accompanying grace already on the road. God will meet him here; Isaac remains responsible for the next step—Egypt or the land the Lord will name.
verses.reformedNotes:
History rhymes: famine again, Gerar again, a Philistine king again. The son’s path retraces the father’s under the same God.

Providence, not accident, places Isaac in Gerar. The field of the next word—and the next failure—is appointed.

verses.text: The LORD appeared to him, and said, “Don’t go down into Egypt. Live in the land I will tell you about.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord appears and forbids Egypt. Isaac must dwell where God will specify—a genuine command, not a hint.

For the hearer: grace initiates by appearing and speaking. The call to stay is sincere and can be obeyed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Appearance precedes strategy. God blocks the Egypt road Abraham once took and claims the right to name Isaac’s dwelling.

Vocation is God’s speech. Isaac will remain because the Lord has appeared, not because famine logic is wiser.

verses.text: Live in this land, and I will be with you, and will bless you. For I will give to you, and to your offspring, all these lands, and I will establish the oath which I swore to Abraham your father.
verses.arminianNotes:
Sojourn, presence, blessing, land, and the oath sworn to Abraham are stacked as God’s “I will.” The promise is sincerely given to Isaac as to his father.

Arminians detect a living covenant word meant to be trusted. Grace accompanies the sojourner; Isaac is invited to stay under a pledge that is not theater.
verses.reformedNotes:
God will be with him, bless him, give the lands, and establish the oath He already swore. The son’s future is the father’s oath kept.

God establishes what He swore. Presence and blessing are covenant initiative, not Isaac’s bargaining chip.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear Abraham’s oath now spoken to Isaac. Arminians press a sincere pledge that accompanies and calls for trust; Calvinists press that God Himself establishes the oath He swore—sure mercy, not Isaac’s merit.

verses.text: I will multiply your offspring as the stars of the sky, and will give all these lands to your offspring. In your offspring all the nations of the earth will be blessed,
verses.arminianNotes:
Stars, lands, and worldwide blessing restated over Isaac. The nations are in view from the son’s generation, not only the father’s.

The blessing aimed at the nations is sincerely held out. In the offspring—later, the Seed—God opens a gift the families of the earth are called to receive.
verses.reformedNotes:
Multiplication, land, and global blessing are God’s “I will” again. The Abrahamic gospel is restated as Isaac’s inheritance.

All nations blessed in the offspring is promise God will keep. The scope is as sure as the Speaker.

verses.text: because Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my requirements, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The “because” names Abraham’s obedience—voice, charge, commandments, statutes, laws—as the historical ground of this confirmation.

Covenant kindness is not wages, yet Abraham’s grace-enabled obedience is not a fiction. Isaac receives a word that honors a father’s kept trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
Abraham’s obedience is cited as covenant history, not as Isaac’s merit. The oath rests on what God swore and on the servant He formed.

“Because Abraham obeyed” is God’s own accounting of the father, not a ladder Isaac must climb. Blessing flows from sworn mercy through a faithful servant.

verses.arminianNotes:
He settles as told. The appearance becomes an address.

Classical Arminians honor the obedience: grace enabled him to stay. Remaining in Gerar is a responsible yes to the word of verses 2–3.
verses.reformedNotes:
Settlement is the firstfruit of the appearance. Isaac is where God placed him.

The sojourn is obedience produced by the Lord’s speech. Gerar is now the appointed stage.

verses.text: The men of the place asked him about his wife. He said, “She is my sister,” for he was afraid to say, “My wife”, lest, he thought, “the men of the place might kill me for Rebekah, because she is beautiful to look at.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The father’s ruse returns: “She is my sister,” from fear of death over Rebekah’s beauty. The lie is named as fear, not as wisdom.

This is culpable unbelief under a still-fresh promise. “I will be with you” was just spoken; Isaac remains responsible for the deceit.
verses.reformedNotes:
Fear scripts the same half-truth Abraham used in Egypt and Gerar. Rebekah, like Sarah, is put at risk in a foreign court.

Election does not make Isaac flawless. God will have to keep the marriage, because Isaac’s word has jeopardized it.

verses.text: When he had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out at a window, and saw, and, behold, Isaac was caressing Rebekah, his wife.
verses.arminianNotes:
Time exposes what fear hid. Abimelech sees marital intimacy—laughing with his wife—and the cover fails.

Pastorally: hidden schemes do not stay hidden. Grace had given years in Gerar; Isaac’s pretense still needed truth.
verses.reformedNotes:
Providence uses a king’s window. The laughter that belongs to marriage becomes the means of uncovering.

God can expose His own servant for the promise’s sake. The long stay is the stage of disclosure, not wasted time.

verses.text: Abimelech called Isaac, and said, “Behold, surely she is your wife. Why did you say, ‘She is my sister’?” Isaac said to him, “Because I said, ‘Lest I die because of her.’”
verses.arminianNotes:
The pagan king catechizes the heir: she is your wife—how then the sister-lie? Isaac answers with the thought of death.

Arminian readers let the rebuke stand. Fear of dying is not an excuse; it is a confession of unbelief Isaac must own.
verses.reformedNotes:
Abimelech names the fact God already knew. Isaac’s defense is the same calculus Abraham used: I thought I would die.

The man of the oath still reasoned from death, not from “I will be with you.” Providence unmasks him without discarding him.

verses.text: Abimelech said, “What is this you have done to us? One of the people might easily have lain with your wife, and you would have brought guilt on us!”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Done to us” and “guilt on us”—the king sees communal harm. Adultery nearly imported by the sojourner’s ruse.

Neighbor-love was breached. A pagan court can still name guilt; Isaac’s scheme endangered people who did not share his covenant.
verses.reformedNotes:
Abimelech fears guilt more than Isaac feared God in verse 7. “One of the people” names a near-sin against marriage and against the Philistine house.

Common grace and conscience can shame the heir of promise. God uses a Gentile king to protect Rebekah and to name the wrong.

verses.text: Abimelech commanded all the people, saying, “He who touches this man or his wife will surely be put to death.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king draws a death-line around Isaac and Rebekah. Pagan authority restrains the very harm Isaac feared.

God can check a court by a king’s edict. Preventing grace here runs through a Gentile warning Isaac did not deserve.
verses.reformedNotes:
Royal decree becomes the wall around the marriage. Touch will mean death—protection Abraham also needed in chapter 20.

The Lord can govern Gerar by a Philistine mouth. Preservation of the line is God’s work, even when the instrument is a pagan ban.

verses.text: Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. The LORD blessed him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Same-year hundredfold is not climate luck; “the Lord blessed him.” Fruitfulness is gift in the land of sojourn.

Wesleyan Arminians receive the harvest as sincere kindness. Blessing accompanies the man who stayed; it does not baptize the earlier lie.
verses.reformedNotes:
Sowing meets a hundredfold because the Lord blessed him—the “I will bless you” of verse 3 now in the barn.

Covenant initiative shows in grain. The Giver, not Gerar’s soil alone, explains the yield.

verses.text: The man grew great, and grew more and more until he became very great.
verses.arminianNotes:
Increase stacks: rich, then more, then very wealthy. Material gift is true and can test the heart as surely as famine did.

Wealth is not automatic holiness. Grace that enriches still calls Isaac to trust the Giver rather than the flocks.
verses.reformedNotes:
The blessing has a public shape: mounting wealth. God makes the promise visible in Isaac’s substance.

“grew more and more” is providence, not Isaac’s Midas touch. The Lord who swore presence is now openly prospering His man.

verses.text: He had possessions of flocks, possessions of herds, and a great household. The Philistines envied him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Isaac’s flocks, herds, and servants multiply, and so does the Philistines’ envy. Gift becomes a social wound. The neighbors’ jealousy is a moral response Isaac must live with.

Prosperity under God does not undo neighbor-tension. Envy is their choice; Isaac will need wisdom, not triumphalism.
verses.reformedNotes:
Possessions trigger Philistine envy. The blessing of verse 3 now draws hostility, as it will again at the wells.

Even envy sits under providence. God can use a neighbor’s jealousy to move the heir toward the next word and the next well.

verses.text: Now all the wells which his father’s servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines had stopped, and filled with earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
Parenthesis of spite: Abraham’s wells filled with earth. Memory of the father is literally blocked.

People can resist a blessing they did not dig. The filled wells are responsible hostility; Isaac will have to reopen what envy buried.
verses.reformedNotes:
Stopping the wells is an attack on life in a dry land—and on Abraham’s footprint. The son’s story inherits the father’s conflicts.

Providence has allowed the filling. The next stage of the oath will include reclaiming water God already gave through Abraham.

verses.text: Abimelech said to Isaac, “Go away from us, for you are much mightier than we.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Expulsion: go away; you are mightier. Fear of Isaac’s strength ends the stay the Lord had blessed.

Wesleyan Arminians see a political choice by Abimelech and a departure Isaac must make. Grace will go with him; the sending-away is still a wound.
verses.reformedNotes:
Might that comes from blessing now unnerves Gerar. The king who protected the marriage cannot tolerate the wealth.

Comfort: exile from Gerar does not void “I will be with you.” Even being sent away can serve the oath God is establishing.
